questions.title: POETRY – ESSAY QUESTION: 'Motho Ke Motho Ka Batho Babang' – Jeremy Cronin
questions.passageText:
By holding my mirror out of the window I see
Clear to the end of the passage.
There's a person down there.
A prisoner polishing a doorhandle.
In the mirror I see him see
My face in the mirror,
I see the fingertips of his free hand
Bunch together, as if to make
An object the size of a badge
Which travels up to his forehead
The place of an imaginary cap.
                        (This means: A warder.)
Two fingers are extended in a vee
And wiggle like two antennae.
                        (He's being watched.)
A finger of his free hand makes a watch-hand's arc
On the wrist of his polishing arm without
Disrupting the slow-slow rhythm of his work.
                        (Later. Maybe, later we can speak.)
Hey! Wat maak jy daar?
                        –a voice from around the corner.
No. Just polishing baas.
He turns his back to me, now watch
His free hand, the talkative one,
Slips quietly behind
                        –Strength brother, it says,
In my mirror,
                        A black fist.

subQuestions.questionText:
With close reference to diction, imagery and structure, write an essay in which you discuss how the speaker conveys the concept of 'ubuntu'/'botho' (communal identity) in this poem.

Your response should take the form of a well-constructed essay of 250–300 words (about ONE page).
subQuestions.memoText:
Use the following, among other points, as a guide:
- The title is a Sesotho/Tswana proverb meaning 'A person is a person through other people', immediately establishing the ubuntu theme of the poem.
- The poem uses everyday communal activities to show how human identity is formed through interaction with others rather than in isolation.
- The use of present participles and action verbs creates a sense of continuous, shared activity, reinforcing the idea that community is not a static state but an ongoing process.
- The frequent use of 'we'/'our' and collective actions emphasises that the individual exists as part of a broader community.
- The poem celebrates ordinary South African life — work, song, dance — as the building blocks of shared identity.
- The loose, organic structure with irregular line lengths mirrors the natural, inclusive quality of communal life; ubuntu cannot be constrained by rigid forms.
- The poem uses vivid sensory imagery (visual, auditory) to evoke the richness and warmth of communal experience.
- The absence of a strict rhyme scheme suggests that ubuntu is open and welcoming, not imposed.
- The poem can be read as a political statement reclaiming and affirming South African communal values in the context of apartheid, which sought to divide people.
- The final lines bring together the various strands of communal activity, affirming that meaning is created collectively.

Refer to rubric in Appendix A (10 marks: Content 6 marks, Structure and Language 4 marks).
Credit valid alternative responses.

questions.title: POETRY – CONTEXTUAL QUESTION: 'First Day after the War' – Mazisi Kunene
questions.passageText:
We heard the songs of a wedding party.
We saw a soft light
Coiling round the young blades of grass
At first we hesitated, then we saw her footprints,
Her face emerged, then her eyes of freedom!
She woke us up with a smile saying,
'What day is this that comes suddenly?'
We said, 'It is the first day after the war'.
Then without waiting we ran to the open space
Ululating to the mountains and the pathways
Calling people from all the circles of the earth.
We shook up the old man demanding a festival
We asked for all the first fruits of the season.
We held hands with a stranger
We shouted across the waterfalls
People came from all lands
It was the first day of peace.
We saw our Ancestors travelling tall on the horizon.

subQuestions.questionText: What does the word 'luminous' (line 1) suggest about the mood of the poem?
subQuestions.memoText:
'Luminous' conveys a mood of radiant joy and hope. It suggests that the first day after the war is not merely bright but filled with an almost sacred, glowing light. This emphasises the sense of renewal and celebration that liberation brings.

Award 2 marks for two distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to the lines in which people emerge and celebrate.

Explain how the atmosphere of freedom is created in these lines.
subQuestions.memoText:
The atmosphere of freedom is created through the image of people emerging from their homes/hiding places and gathering together. The communal celebration — singing, dancing and shouting — creates a joyful, exuberant atmosphere. The sense of release from oppression is palpable as the community reclaims public space.

Award 1 mark for identifying the atmosphere and 1 mark for an explanation.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how the imagery of dawn and light contributes to the meaning of the poem.
subQuestions.memoText:
The imagery of dawn and light is used to symbolise the arrival of a new era. Dawn represents the end of darkness (oppression, war, fear) and the beginning of a new day (freedom, peace, hope). The light imagery is associated with clarity and truth — after the obscuring darkness of war, everything is now visible and open. This imagery reinforces the central message that liberation is not merely political but also spiritual and transformative.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well developed.

subQuestions.questionText: Critically discuss how the poem conveys the significance of communal celebration in the context of liberation.
subQuestions.memoText:
The poem presents communal celebration as the natural and necessary response to liberation. By emphasising that people celebrate together — through shared music, dance, and gathering — Kunene suggests that freedom is not experienced individually but collectively. The communal dimension of the celebration validates the communal nature of the struggle: suffering and liberation are shared experiences. The poem also implies that the act of celebration is itself an assertion of humanity and dignity that had been suppressed during the war/apartheid. The collective joy is an affirmation of survival and resilience.

Award 3 marks for a critical discussion.

questions.title: POETRY – CONTEXTUAL QUESTION: 'Funeral Blues' – W.H. Auden
questions.passageText:
Stop all the clocks, cut off the telephone,
Prevent the dog from barking with a juicy bone,
Silence the pianos and with muffled drum
Bring out the coffin, let the mourners come.

Let aeroplanes circle moaning overhead
Scribbling on the sky the message 'He is Dead'.
Put crepe bows round the white necks of the public doves,
Let the traffic policemen wear black cotton gloves.

He was my North, my South, my East and West,
My working week and my Sunday rest,
My noon, my midnight, my talk, my song;
I thought that love would last forever: I was wrong.

The stars are not wanted now; put out every one,
Pack up the moon and dismantle the sun,
Pour away the ocean and sweep up the wood;
For nothing now can ever come to any good.

subQuestions.questionText: What does the phrase 'muffled drum' (line 3) suggest about the speaker's state of mind?
subQuestions.memoText:
'Muffled' suggests that the normally vibrant, celebratory sound of the drum has been suppressed and silenced. This reflects the speaker's overwhelming grief — all joy and vitality must be subdued in acknowledgement of the loss. The drum, usually associated with celebration, is now a symbol of mourning.

Award 2 marks for two distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to lines 5–6: 'Let aeroplanes circle moaning overhead, / Scribbling on the sky the message He Is Dead.'

Explain the effect of capitalising 'He Is Dead'.
subQuestions.memoText:
The capitalisation elevates the announcement to something of cosmic or royal importance. It suggests the death should be proclaimed to the world as a momentous event. The speaker's grief is so profound that he believes the entire world must be informed and must stop to acknowledge this loss, as one would for a head of state or a divine figure.

Award 2 marks for two distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to lines 9–11: 'He was my North, my South, my East and West, / My working week and my Sunday rest, / My noon, my midnight, my talk, my song.'

Discuss the effectiveness of the metaphors in these lines.
subQuestions.memoText:
The directional metaphors (North/South/East/West) suggest that the deceased gave the speaker's life direction, purpose and orientation. Without him, the speaker is lost. The contrast between 'working week' and 'Sunday rest' implies that the deceased was present in every aspect of the speaker's life — both mundane and special. 'Noon' and 'midnight' further extends this to every moment of the day. The anaphora of 'My' creates a cumulative, obsessive effect that conveys the totality of the speaker's dependence on and love for the deceased.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well developed.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to stanza 4: 'The stars are not wanted now … come to any good.'

Critically discuss how this stanza conveys the central message of the poem.
subQuestions.memoText:
The final stanza is the most nihilistic and all-consuming expression of grief in the poem. The speaker dismisses the entire natural world — stars, moon, ocean, wood — as irrelevant now that the beloved is gone. The forceful commands ('put out', 'pack up', 'dismantle', 'pour away', 'sweep up') demonstrate a desire to erase all beauty from existence. The final line — 'For nothing now can ever come to any good' — encapsulates the central message: that love is so total that its loss makes life itself meaningless. The poem ultimately critiques the idea that grief can be contained or that life simply continues after profound loss.

Award 3 marks for a critical discussion.

questions.title: POETRY – CONTEXTUAL QUESTION: 'Felix Randal' – Gerard Manley Hopkins
questions.passageText:
Felix Randal the farrier, O is he dead then? my duty all ended,
Who have watched his mould of man, big-boned and hardy-handsome
Pining, pining, till time when reason rambled in it, and some
Fatal four disorders, fleshed there, all contended?

Sickness broke him. Impatient, he cursed at first, but mended
Being anointed and all; though a heavenlier heart began some
Months earlier, since I had our sweet reprieve and ransom
Tendered to him. Ah well, God rest him all road ever he offended!

This seeing the sick endears them to us, us too it endears.
My tongue had taught thee comfort, touch had quenched thy tears,
Thy tears that touched my heart, child, Felix, poor Felix Randal;

How far from then forethought of, all thy more boisterous years,
When thou at the random grim forge, powerful amidst peers,
Didst fettle for the great grey drayhorse his bright and battering sandal!

subQuestions.questionText: What does the compound phrase 'big-boned and hardy-handsome' (line 2) reveal about Felix Randal?
subQuestions.memoText:
The compound phrase reveals that Felix was physically imposing and powerfully built, with a robust, healthy appearance. It emphasises his physical vitality and strength before his illness, creating a poignant contrast with his subsequent weakness and death.

Award 2 marks for two distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to line 1: 'Felix Randal the farrier, O is he dead then? my duty all ended,'

Explain the tone of this opening line.
subQuestions.memoText:
The tone is questioning and reflective, suggesting a moment of sudden realisation. The exclamation 'O' conveys a flash of shock and sorrow at Felix's death. The comment 'my duty all ended' suggests the speaker is processing the loss as he speaks, yet also implies that his professional obligation has ceased while his personal connection lingers.

Award 2 marks for two distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how the tone shifts between the octave (lines 1–8) and the sestet (lines 9–14) of the poem.
subQuestions.memoText:
In the octave, the speaker adopts a relatively professional, somewhat detached tone as he recounts Felix's illness and his role in administering last rites. The language is controlled and theological. However, in the sestet, the tone becomes warmer, more personal and elegiac. The intimate address 'child, Felix, poor Felix Randal' reveals a deep affection that transcends the priest's professional role. The sestet shows that the relationship had grown into genuine human care and love, making the loss personal rather than merely dutiful.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well developed.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to the final couplet: 'When thou at the random grim forge, powerful amidst peers, / Didst fettle for the great grey drayhorse his bright and battering sandal!'

Critically discuss how this ending contributes to the poem's meaning.
subQuestions.memoText:
The final couplet returns to Felix in his prime — powerful, skilled and purposeful at his forge. The image of him fashioning a horseshoe for a working horse represents Felix at the height of his vitality and craft. 'Bright and battering' conveys both the beauty and the force of his work, celebrating the dignity of physical labour. The poem ends not on death or weakness but on life and strength. This retrospective vision suggests that Felix's identity was defined by his work and vigour, not by his suffering. The exclamation mark conveys admiration and even joy, ensuring Felix is remembered as a whole, capable man rather than merely a dying patient.

Award 3 marks for a critical discussion.

questions.title: UNSEEN POETRY (COMPULSORY) – CONTEXTUAL QUESTION: 'Burning the Fire Break' – Ingrid Andersen

subQuestions.questionText: What does the title 'Burning the Fire Break' suggest about the poem's central concern?
subQuestions.memoText:
The title refers to the controlled burning of a strip of land (fire break) to prevent the spread of wildfire. This suggests a central concern with controlled destruction: the idea that deliberate burning (destruction) can prevent greater, uncontrolled devastation. The title introduces a tension between destruction and protection.

Award 2 marks for two distinct points.
subQuestions.topic: Unseen Poetry – Title and Central Concern

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how the atmosphere of tension and anticipation is created in the poem.
subQuestions.memoText:
The atmosphere of tension is created through imagery of controlled fire — the deliberate, calculated nature of the burning creates a sense of danger and uncertainty. The anticipation of the fire spreading or being contained dominates the poem. Short, declarative sentences and active verbs reinforce a sense of urgency and careful attention to a potentially dangerous situation.

Award 1 mark for identifying the atmosphere and 1 mark for an explanation.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the effectiveness of the fire imagery throughout the poem.
subQuestions.memoText:
The fire imagery is central to the poem's exploration of the paradox of controlled destruction. Fire is simultaneously a destructive and a purifying force — it clears the land, removes dead growth, and prepares for renewal. The imagery of flames, smoke and ash reinforces this duality. The controlled, purposeful nature of the burning contrasts with the threat of uncontrolled wildfire, suggesting that destruction can be both intentional and ultimately beneficial. The fire imagery is thus effective in carrying the poem's thematic weight about the necessity of painful transformation.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well developed.

subQuestions.questionText: Critically discuss how the poem uses the controlled burning of a fire break as a metaphor for a broader human or emotional experience.
subQuestions.memoText:
The poem uses the fire break as a metaphor for the idea that controlled sacrifice or loss can prevent greater devastation. On a human level, this could represent the necessity of letting go of something painful (relationships, past experiences, old ways) to prevent greater suffering. The burning is presented not as random destruction but as a deliberate, purposeful act — suggesting that conscious, difficult choices are sometimes necessary for survival and renewal. The poem ultimately argues that controlled destruction can be an act of care and wisdom rather than merely an act of violence.

Award 3 marks for a critical discussion.
subQuestions.topic: Unseen Poetry – Extended Metaphor and Meaning

questions.title: THE PICTURE OF DORIAN GRAY – ESSAY QUESTION (Oscar Wilde)

subQuestions.questionText:
It is through his relationships with others that Dorian Gray's true character is both revealed and destroyed.

Critically discuss this statement.

Your response should take the form of a well-constructed essay of 400–450 words (2–2½ pages).
subQuestions.memoText:
Use the following as a guideline:
- Dorian's relationship with Basil Hallward is foundational: Basil's adoration and the creation of the portrait ignite Dorian's vanity and his obsessive desire to preserve his youth and beauty at any cost.
- Lord Henry's influence is arguably the most destructive relationship in the novel. His hedonistic and aesthetic philosophy provides Dorian with a framework for rejecting morality and conscience. Lord Henry's witty aphorisms give Dorian permission to pursue pleasure without restraint.
- The gift of the yellow book by Lord Henry serves as a blueprint for Dorian's corrupt lifestyle and effectively seals his moral fate.
- Dorian's relationship with Sibyl Vane initially suggests the possibility of genuine love and redemption. However, his cruel rejection of her after her 'failed' performance reveals his shallowness and incapacity for real emotional connection. Sibyl's subsequent suicide marks the first sign of the portrait's corruption.
- Dorian's relationships become increasingly exploitative and cruel. He treats people — Alan Campbell, James Vane's social circle, Lady Gwendolyn's family — with contempt and callousness, using them for his own ends and discarding them.
- His relationship with Basil ends in murder, representing the ultimate destruction of the one person who genuinely cared for his soul rather than his appearance.
- Even his relationship with Lord Henry, which appears to survive, is built on a fundamental deception — Lord Henry never suspects the depths of Dorian's depravity.
- The portrait, which records the true state of Dorian's soul, functions as a kind of relationship with himself. His final act of stabbing the portrait destroys both the record of his corruption and, ultimately, himself.
- Dorian's inability to form genuine, ethical relationships is both a symptom and a cause of his moral destruction.

Credit valid alternative responses.
Refer to Sections B and C rubric (25 marks: Content 15 marks, Structure and Language 10 marks).

questions.title: THE PICTURE OF DORIAN GRAY – CONTEXTUAL QUESTION (Oscar Wilde)

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Extract A.

Explain the circumstances that have brought Lord Henry and Dorian together at this point in the novel.
subQuestions.memoText:
Basil Hallward has invited Lord Henry to his studio while he paints Dorian's portrait. Basil is reluctant to introduce them as he fears Lord Henry's corrupting influence on Dorian's pure character. However, the introduction takes place. Lord Henry immediately becomes fascinated by Dorian's youth and beauty and begins to exert his philosophical influence on the impressionable young man.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss what Lord Henry's speeches in Extract A reveal about his character and his philosophy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Lord Henry reveals himself to be a sophisticated, witty but morally hollow character. His philosophy is hedonistic and aesthetic — he values beauty, pleasure and sensation above all else, dismissing conventional morality as limiting. He is manipulative in the way he shapes Dorian's thinking, presenting vice as attractive and wisdom. His character is defined by a paradox: he is highly intelligent yet uses that intelligence to corrupt rather than guide. He is an armchair philosopher who advocates excess without actually living it himself.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Basil's attitude toward Dorian in Extract A.

Discuss the contrast between Basil's and Lord Henry's relationships with Dorian.
subQuestions.memoText:
Basil's relationship with Dorian is protective, genuinely admiring and spiritually invested — he sees Dorian as his artistic ideal and wants to preserve his innocence. Lord Henry, by contrast, treats Dorian as an intellectual experiment and an object to be shaped according to his own philosophy. Basil's love for Dorian is selfless while Lord Henry's interest is self-serving. This contrast highlights the tension between genuine care and manipulative influence that underpins the novel.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Critically discuss the irony evident in Dorian's wish that the portrait would age instead of him.
subQuestions.memoText:
The irony is layered and profound. Dorian wishes for eternal youth believing it will bring him freedom and happiness. However, the granting of his wish traps him in a kind of living death — he is unable to grow, change or mature morally because he faces no physical consequences for his actions. The portrait, which ages and degrades, becomes the true mirror of his soul — more honest than his youthful face. Ironically, the wish that seemed to free him from time enslaves him to his secret. The portrait ultimately destroys him, turning his apparent gift into a curse.

Award 3 marks for a critical discussion.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Extract B.

Explain what has happened to bring Dorian to the state described in this extract.
subQuestions.memoText:
Dorian has spent years living a dissolute life under the influence of Lord Henry's philosophy and the yellow book. He has been responsible for the ruin of many lives, including Sibyl Vane's, Alan Campbell's and Basil's murder. The portrait has grown increasingly hideous as a record of his sins. Despite outward appearances of youth and beauty, Dorian is consumed by guilt and moral corruption.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss what Dorian's attitude toward the portrait in Extract B reveals about his psychological state.
subQuestions.memoText:
Dorian's attitude toward the portrait reveals a character torn between guilt and self-deception. He is horrified by what the portrait reveals about his soul, yet he cannot escape it. His attempts to hide or destroy the portrait suggest a desperate desire to deny his own corruption. The portrait functions as his conscience — a conscience he tries to ignore but cannot silence. His psychological state is one of increasing paranoia, self-loathing and moral disintegration.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how Oscar Wilde uses the portrait as a symbol of moral conscience in the novel as a whole.
subQuestions.memoText:
The portrait is the central symbol of the novel, functioning as Dorian's externalised conscience. While Dorian's face remains young and innocent, the portrait records every sin and moral failing in grotesque physical detail. This allows Wilde to make visible the normally invisible consequences of a life without moral accountability. The portrait represents the Dorian Wilde believes should exist — a self that is held to account. When Dorian finally stabs the portrait, he believes he can destroy his conscience, but instead destroys himself, suggesting that the conscience cannot be killed without destroying the self.

Award 3 marks for a well-developed discussion.

subQuestions.questionText: Using Extract B as a starting point, and drawing on your knowledge of the novel as a whole, critically discuss whether Dorian Gray is ultimately a sympathetic or an unsympathetic character.
subQuestions.memoText:
SYMPATHETIC:
- Dorian is, in part, a victim of forces beyond his control. Lord Henry's manipulation and Basil's adoration together create the conditions for his corruption at a young, impressionable age.
- He shows moments of genuine remorse and self-awareness — his attempted attempt at virtue with Hetty Merton demonstrates some desire for redemption.
- His youth and innocence at the start of the novel make readers invested in what he could have become.
- He is aware of his own degradation, which distinguishes him from purely villainous characters.

UNSYMPATHETIC:
- Dorian makes a series of wilful, cruel choices that destroy others. His treatment of Sibyl, his murder of Basil, his blackmailing of Alan Campbell cannot be excused by his upbringing or influences.
- He lacks genuine empathy. His concern for others is always secondary to his self-preservation and desire for pleasure.
- He has ample opportunity to reform but consistently chooses corruption.
- His good looks and charm make him more dangerous — he uses his attractiveness to deceive and exploit.

Credit valid mixed responses.
Award 4 marks for a well-developed critical discussion that engages with the novel as a whole.

questions.title: LIFE OF PI – ESSAY QUESTION (Yann Martel)

subQuestions.questionText:
Pi's faith is his greatest source of strength throughout the novel.

Critically discuss this statement.

Your response should take the form of a well-constructed essay of 400–450 words (2–2½ pages).
subQuestions.memoText:
Use the following as a guideline:
- Pi's multi-faith identity (Hinduism, Christianity, Islam) gives him a richly layered spiritual framework. Rather than creating conflict, his simultaneous practice of three religions deepens his sense of connection to the divine.
- His faith provides him with a structured daily routine at sea — prayer, meditation and ritual give meaning and order to an otherwise chaotic existence on the lifeboat.
- Pi's conviction that God is present even in the darkest moments sustains his will to survive. When survival seems impossible, faith provides the psychological endurance to continue.
- The algae island episode tests Pi's faith: he recognises the island's illusory comfort and chooses to leave, a decision guided by his deeper conviction that a meaningful life requires active engagement with the world, not passive withdrawal.
- Pi's ability to reinterpret his horrific experience through a narrative lens (the animal story) can itself be seen as an act of faith — a choice to believe in a story that preserves human dignity.
- At the same time, faith is tested severely. The suffering Pi endures — starvation, violence, the loss of his family — challenges any simple belief in a benevolent God.
- Pi's pragmatic adaptation (eating meat, killing) could be seen as a departure from his religious principles, suggesting that survival sometimes supersedes faith.
- The novel's central question — which story do you prefer? — is itself a question about faith: the willingness to believe in a story that makes life more meaningful, even without definitive proof.
- Candidates might argue that Pi's ingenuity, resourcefulness and psychological resilience — not faith alone — account for his survival.

Credit valid alternative/mixed responses.
Refer to Sections B and C rubric (25 marks: Content 15 marks, Structure and Language 10 marks).

questions.title: LIFE OF PI – CONTEXTUAL QUESTION (Yann Martel)

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Extract C.

Explain the circumstances that have brought Pi to the situation described in this extract.
subQuestions.memoText:
The Tsimtsum, the cargo ship carrying Pi's family and their zoo animals to Canada, has sunk in the Pacific Ocean. Pi has managed to get onto the lifeboat, where he finds himself sharing the space with a Bengal tiger named Richard Parker. Pi's family and most of the other animals have perished. Pi must now survive alone on the open ocean with a dangerous predator.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss what Pi's response to Richard Parker in Extract C reveals about his character.
subQuestions.memoText:
Pi's response to Richard Parker reveals his resourcefulness, pragmatism and intelligence. Rather than surrendering to fear, Pi draws on his knowledge of animal behaviour (learned from growing up in a zoo) to establish dominance and manage the tiger. This reveals a character who can think clearly under extreme pressure and who converts fear into strategic action. It also reveals Pi's fundamental belief that survival requires adaptation and creative problem-solving.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the significance of Richard Parker's name in the context of the novel as a whole.
subQuestions.memoText:
The name 'Richard Parker' is significant because it humanises the tiger, blurring the boundary between human and animal. It also alludes to a historical/literary figure — there are several real Richard Parkers associated with survival at sea and cannibalism, subtly foreshadowing the darker events in Pi's story. The name contributes to the novel's central ambiguity: if Richard Parker is Pi's alter ego or psychological coping mechanism, then naming him humanises the savage, survival-driven side of Pi that he cannot otherwise acknowledge.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well developed.

subQuestions.questionText: Critically discuss how Extract C contributes to the novel's exploration of the relationship between fear and survival.
subQuestions.memoText:
Extract C illustrates that fear, when channelled correctly, becomes a survival tool. Pi's fear of Richard Parker keeps him alert, disciplined and focused — without this fear, he might have lapsed into passivity and died. Martel suggests that the relationship between predator and prey is not simply one of danger but of mutual dependency: Pi needs the tiger's presence as a reason to survive and maintain structure in his life. Fear thus becomes productive and purposeful, contradicting the instinct to flee. The novel argues that the confrontation with one's deepest fear is a prerequisite for genuine survival.

Award 3 marks for a critical discussion.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Extract D.

Explain why Pi offers the Japanese investigators 'another story'.
subQuestions.memoText:
The Japanese shipping officials are sceptical of Pi's story involving animals, dismissing it as implausible and unhelpful for their official report. They demand a more realistic, factual account of the shipwreck. Pi therefore provides an alternative story — one in which the animals are replaced by human characters — to satisfy their need for a conventional narrative.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss what the Japanese investigators' preference for the 'human' story reveals about human psychology.
subQuestions.memoText:
The investigators' preference for the human story — which is actually more brutal and disturbing — reveals the paradox of human psychology: people often prefer a plausible, realistic account even when it involves greater suffering, over an implausible story that is more comforting. It suggests that human beings are conditioned to distrust the miraculous or the extraordinary. Their preference also reveals how adults impose rational frameworks on experience, rejecting narratives that do not fit conventional understanding. Ironically, the 'rational' story is harder to bear emotionally than the animal story.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the significance of the question 'Which story do you prefer?' in the context of the novel's central theme.
subQuestions.memoText:
This question is the novel's thematic heart: it invites the reader to choose between a factual but devastating account and a beautiful but unverifiable story. Martel uses this to explore the nature of faith and belief — the willingness to prefer the story that gives life meaning, even without proof. The question implies that the stories we choose to believe shape our experience of reality. If Richard Parker represents Pi's survival instinct and the animal story is his coping mechanism, then preferring it is an act of compassion toward the self. The question also implicates the reader, asking whether we too prefer the 'better' story.

Award 3 marks for a well-developed discussion.
subQuestions.topic: Novel – Faith, Narrative and Central Theme

subQuestions.questionText: Using Extract D as a starting point, and drawing on your knowledge of the novel as a whole, critically discuss whether Pi is a reliable narrator.
subQuestions.memoText:
UNRELIABLE:
- Pi presents two contradictory stories. This immediately raises questions about which, if either, is true, and what Pi has omitted or altered.
- If the human story is the 'real' one, then Pi has fabricated the animal story — he is deliberately misleading the reader with a more palatable fiction.
- Pi's survival under extraordinary circumstances is so remarkable that readers are invited to doubt his account.
- The framing narrative (the novelist interviewing the adult Pi) adds another layer of distance and potential distortion.

RELIABLE:
- Pi's account is internally consistent and detailed; he provides explanations for practical challenges of survival.
- The Japanese officials acknowledge that Pi's survival is factually documented.
- The ambiguity may be intentional: Martel refuses to resolve the question, suggesting both stories can be simultaneously 'true' in different registers (literal vs. psychological).
- Pi is honest about the limits of memory and trauma, which is itself a marker of reliability.

Credit valid mixed responses.
Award 4 marks for a well-developed critical discussion that engages with the novel as a whole.

subQuestions.questionText:
Hamlet's inability to act decisively is the primary cause of the tragedy in the play.

Critically discuss this statement.

Your response should take the form of a well-constructed essay of 400–450 words (2–2½ pages).
subQuestions.memoText:
AGREE:
- Hamlet is tasked with avenging his father's murder from early in the play, yet delays action through the majority of the drama. This procrastination allows Claudius time to consolidate his power and plan counter-measures.
- Hamlet's philosophical nature leads him to overthink his task. His famous 'To be or not to be' soliloquy reveals a character paralysed by existential doubt rather than spurred to action.
- His decision to stage 'The Mousetrap' to confirm Claudius's guilt — rather than acting on the ghost's word — represents a delay that costs lives.
- When Hamlet has the opportunity to kill Claudius at prayer, he hesitates for theological reasons (he does not want to send Claudius to heaven). This is perhaps his most costly missed opportunity.
- His mistaken killing of Polonius leads directly to Ophelia's madness and death and Laertes's desire for revenge — consequences of impulsive, misdirected action rather than considered decisiveness.
- Hamlet's sending of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to their deaths shows he is capable of decisive action when not paralysed by conscience, yet he applies this decisiveness inconsistently.
- The final scene's bloodbath — the deaths of Gertrude, Laertes, Claudius and Hamlet himself — could have been avoided had Hamlet acted earlier.

DISAGREE / QUALIFYING:
- Hamlet's caution is justified: he needs proof before committing regicide. A hasty, unverified revenge would have made him a murderer, not an avenger of justice.
- The tragedy is partly caused by external forces — Claudius's treachery, the poisoned sword, Gertrude's unwitting drinking of the poisoned wine — not solely by Hamlet's character.
- Hamlet does act decisively in several instances: the play-within-a-play, his return from England, his killing of Claudius at the end.
- The corrupt state of Denmark (the 'something rotten') precedes Hamlet's arrival on the scene; the tragedy has structural, political causes beyond any individual's inaction.

Credit valid alternative/mixed responses.
Refer to Sections B and C rubric (25 marks: Content 15 marks, Structure and Language 10 marks).

subQuestions.questionText: Place Extract E in context.
subQuestions.memoText:
Hamlet has just encountered his father's ghost on the battlements, who has revealed that he was murdered by Claudius — his own brother — who poured poison into his ear while he slept. The ghost commands Hamlet to avenge his death. Hamlet is shaken, uncertain and sworn to secrecy. He is now tasked with the burden of revenge while struggling with the authenticity of the ghost's message and its implications for his mother and uncle.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss what Hamlet's soliloquy in Extract E reveals about his state of mind.
subQuestions.memoText:
Hamlet's soliloquy reveals a deeply troubled mind wrestling with conflicting obligations, emotions and beliefs. He is overwhelmed by the revelation of his father's murder and his mother's 'incestuous' remarriage. His thoughts are rapid and disjointed, reflecting emotional turmoil. He is also beginning to formulate the idea of feigning madness as a strategy, suggesting a calculating intelligence beneath the emotional distress. His state of mind oscillates between grief, rage, disgust and determination.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the theme of appearance versus reality as it is evident in Extract E.
subQuestions.memoText:
Extract E is saturated with the tension between appearance and reality. Claudius appears to be a legitimate, mourning king but is in fact a murderer and usurper. Gertrude appears devoted to her new husband but may be complicit in — or ignorant of — his crime. Hamlet himself plans to adopt an 'antic disposition' (feigned madness) — a deliberate gap between appearance and reality. The ghost has revealed that the 'smiling villain' Claudius conceals a corrupt interior beneath a smooth public surface.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Critically discuss whether Hamlet's decision to feign madness is a wise or an unwise strategy.
subQuestions.memoText:
WISE:
- Feigning madness gives Hamlet freedom to say dangerous truths that would otherwise result in punishment or death.
- It allows him time to investigate the truth of the ghost's accusations without arousing suspicion.
- It provides psychological cover — Claudius dismisses Hamlet's accusations as the ravings of a mad prince.

UNWISE:
- The strategy ultimately isolates Hamlet from potential allies and from Ophelia.
- It causes Ophelia's genuine madness and death, contributing to the tragedy.
- It gives Claudius reason to have Hamlet removed from Denmark, nearly resulting in his execution.
- The strategy delays action rather than enabling it.

Accept valid mixed responses.
Award 3 marks for a well-developed discussion.

subQuestions.questionText: Place Extract F in context.
subQuestions.memoText:
Hamlet has returned unexpectedly from England, having discovered and rewritten Claudius's letter ordering his execution in England, substituting Rosencrantz and Guildenstern's names for his own. He has encountered Ophelia's funeral procession and grappled with Laertes in her grave. Claudius has now enlisted Laertes's help to kill Hamlet, planning a fencing match with a poisoned sword.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how Claudius manipulates Laertes in Extract F.
subQuestions.memoText:
Claudius exploits Laertes's grief and fury at his father's death and his sister's madness to direct Laertes's desire for revenge away from himself and toward Hamlet. He frames Hamlet as Laertes's enemy, concealing his own role in Polonius's death (Hamlet killed Polonius in Claudius's presence and with some of Claudius's encouragement). Claudius is careful, flattering and strategic — he praises Laertes's swordsmanship and inflames his honour to secure his cooperation. He uses Laertes as a weapon while protecting himself from direct blame.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how the poisoned sword and the poisoned wine in Extract F reflect the moral corruption at the heart of the play.
subQuestions.memoText:
The poisoned sword and wine are literal embodiments of the corruption that pervades Denmark. Just as Claudius poured poison into King Hamlet's ear, he now arranges for poison to be deployed physically. The poison functions as a symbol of the way evil contaminates everything it touches — the fencing match, meant to appear as an honourable contest, is secretly a trap. The poison ultimately kills not only Hamlet but Gertrude (the innocent bystander) and Laertes himself, suggesting that moral corruption is self-destructive and indiscriminate.

Award 3 marks for a well-developed discussion.

subQuestions.questionText: Using Extract F as a starting point, and drawing on your knowledge of the play as a whole, critically discuss whether Hamlet achieves justice at the end of the play.
subQuestions.memoText:
YES — JUSTICE IS ACHIEVED:
- Claudius is ultimately killed, paying for his murder of King Hamlet. The revenge Hamlet was tasked with is accomplished.
- Laertes, who participates in a treacherous plot, also dies — facing consequences for his willingness to use dishonourable means.
- The full truth of Claudius's crimes is revealed publicly before the court, ensuring that his guilt is known.
- Fortinbras's arrival and assumption of power restores order to Denmark.

NO — JUSTICE IS INCOMPLETE:
- Too many innocent people die — Gertrude, Ophelia, Polonius, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern — for the outcome to be considered just.
- Hamlet himself dies, which means the avenger of justice is also consumed by the vengeance cycle.
- The play raises the question of whether human revenge can ever truly constitute justice, given its collateral damage.
- A truly just outcome would have seen Claudius held accountable without the deaths of the innocent.

Credit valid mixed responses.
Award 4 marks for a well-developed critical discussion that engages with the play as a whole.

subQuestions.questionText:
Othello's greatest strength is also the source of his greatest weakness.

Critically discuss this statement with reference to the play as a whole.

Your response should take the form of a well-constructed essay of 400–450 words (2–2½ pages).
subQuestions.memoText:
Use the following as a guideline:
- Othello's greatest strength is his absolute faith and trust in others. He is open, trusting and incapable of sustained suspicion — qualities that make him an inspiring leader and a devoted husband.
- However, this same openness and trust is exploited by Iago. Because Othello is unable to conceive of sustained deception in those closest to him, he becomes entirely vulnerable to Iago's manipulation.
- His military excellence and decisiveness are legendary. On the battlefield, these qualities make him formidable. In personal relationships, however, his tendency toward swift, decisive judgement leads him to condemn Desdemona on the basis of circumstantial evidence rather than proof.
- Othello's love for Desdemona is intense, passionate and all-consuming — a strength that demonstrates his capacity for deep feeling. Yet this same intensity means that when his love curdles into jealousy, the result is catastrophic. He cannot feel 'a little' jealous; his nature is totalising.
- His sense of honour and dignity is a defining strength: it makes him a respected leader and principled man. Yet when Iago convinces him that his honour has been compromised (via Desdemona's alleged infidelity), this same pride drives him to destructive revenge.
- Othello's outsider status in Venetian society makes him acutely aware of his identity and his achievement. This self-awareness makes him admirable but also vulnerable — Iago exploits his racial and social insecurities to undermine his self-confidence.
- His capacity for remorse at the end ('one that loved not wisely, but too well') reveals the tragedy: Othello possessed the qualities of a great man, but they were turned against him.

Credit valid alternative/mixed responses.
Refer to Sections B and C rubric (25 marks: Content 15 marks, Structure and Language 10 marks).

subQuestions.questionText: Place Extract G in context.
subQuestions.memoText:
Iago has begun his campaign to destroy Othello by planting seeds of suspicion about Desdemona and Cassio. He has insinuated that Cassio is overly familiar with Desdemona and has begun to exploit the handkerchief — the first love token Othello gave Desdemona — as 'proof' of infidelity. Othello, initially resistant, is being drawn deeper into jealousy and is beginning to demand 'ocular proof'.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the techniques Iago uses to manipulate Othello in Extract G.
subQuestions.memoText:
Iago uses calculated insinuation rather than direct accusation — he hints and suggests rather than states, forcing Othello to fill in the gaps with his own imagination. He uses rhetorical questions to undermine Othello's certainty. He feigns reluctance to reveal his suspicions, which paradoxically makes Othello more desperate to hear them. He appeals to Othello's sense of honour, suggesting that a cuckold's position is shameful, to intensify the emotional stakes. His technique is to weaponise Othello's own imagination against him.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the significance of the handkerchief as a symbol in Extract G and in the play as a whole.
subQuestions.memoText:
The handkerchief is Othello's first love token to Desdemona — it represents their love, trust and the bond between them. As a symbol, it carries enormous weight: its loss, engineered by Iago through Emilia, becomes 'evidence' of Desdemona's infidelity. In the play as a whole, the handkerchief demonstrates how Iago transforms innocent objects into instruments of destruction. It also represents the fragility of trust: a small, easily misplaced object becomes the catalyst for murder, suggesting that relationships built without clear communication are dangerously vulnerable to manipulation.

Award 3 marks for a well-developed discussion.

subQuestions.questionText: Critically discuss what Extract G reveals about the relationship between reason and passion in Othello's character.
subQuestions.memoText:
Extract G marks the critical moment when Othello's rational faculties begin to be overwhelmed by passion/jealousy. Initially, Othello resists Iago's insinuations and demands proof — this represents his reason. However, once the seed of suspicion is planted, his passionate nature increasingly displaces reason. The extract shows how jealousy functions as an emotional toxin that corrupts clear thinking. Othello's tragedy is not that he lacks reason but that his passions, when sufficiently inflamed, override it. Iago understands this vulnerability precisely and exploits it.

Award 3 marks for a critical discussion.

subQuestions.questionText: Place Extract H in context.
subQuestions.memoText:
Othello has convinced himself of Desdemona's guilt and has smothered her in their bed. Emilia arrives and discovers what has happened. Through the confrontation with Emilia and Iago, the full truth is revealed: the handkerchief was stolen, not dropped; Cassio is innocent; Iago has been orchestrating everything. Iago kills Emilia to silence her. Othello, understanding the full horror of what he has done, prepares to take his own life.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss what Emilia's role in Extract H reveals about the theme of loyalty.
subQuestions.memoText:
Emilia's actions in Extract H represent a transformative moment in her relationship to loyalty. Throughout the play, Emilia has been loyal to Iago, even unwittingly assisting his scheme by taking the handkerchief. However, when confronted with the consequences of Iago's manipulation and Othello's murder of Desdemona, Emilia chooses loyalty to truth and justice over loyalty to her husband. Her defiance of Iago and her public revelation of his treachery — at the cost of her own life — suggest that genuine loyalty must ultimately serve moral truth rather than personal relationships.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how Othello's final speech in Extract H affects your response to him as a character.
subQuestions.memoText:
Othello's final speech restores some of his dignity and invites a measure of sympathy. His self-assessment — 'one that loved not wisely, but too well' — is honest and self-aware, suggesting he understands the nature of his tragic flaw. His acknowledgement of his past military service and his genuine grief for Desdemona reinstate the noble qualities that existed before Iago's corruption. However, the speech also invites critical scrutiny: some readers find it too composed, too focused on reputation, suggesting that even now Othello is more concerned with how he is perceived than with authentic remorse.

Award 3 marks for a well-developed discussion.
subQuestions.topic: Drama – Character Assessment and Final Speech

subQuestions.questionText: Using Extract H as a starting point, and drawing on your knowledge of the play as a whole, critically discuss to what extent Iago is responsible for the tragedy in Othello.
subQuestions.memoText:
LARGELY RESPONSIBLE:
- Iago orchestrates the entire plot: he engineers the dismissal of Cassio, plants suspicion about Desdemona, steals the handkerchief and manufactures 'ocular proof'.
- Without Iago's intervention, there is no reason to believe Othello and Desdemona's marriage would have failed. Their love is presented as genuine and deep.
- Iago exploits the weaknesses of every character — Roderigo's infatuation, Othello's insecurity, Cassio's vanity, Emilia's obedience — demonstrating exceptional psychological intelligence deployed entirely in the service of malice.
- Iago's motivations (resentment at being passed over for promotion; racial resentment; sexual jealousy) are disproportionate to the devastation he causes.

PARTLY RESPONSIBLE — OTHER FACTORS:
- Othello's insecurity, jealousy and tendency to act without sufficient proof make him complicit in his own destruction. A more emotionally secure character might have resisted Iago's manipulation.
- Venetian society's racial prejudice creates the conditions of insecurity that Iago exploits.
- Roderigo's willingness to fund Iago's scheme and Emilia's taking of the handkerchief (however unwitting) both contribute.
- Desdemona's failure to assert herself clearly in the face of Othello's accusations is a contributing factor.

Credit valid mixed responses.
Award 4 marks for a well-developed critical discussion that engages with the play as a whole.

subQuestions.questionText:
John Proctor's journey from flawed individual to tragic hero is the central concern of The Crucible.

Critically discuss this statement.

Your response should take the form of a well-constructed essay of 400–450 words (2–2½ pages).
subQuestions.memoText:
Use the following as a guideline:
- John Proctor is introduced as a fundamentally decent man but one who has committed adultery with Abigail Williams. This sin defines his character at the start of the play and is the source of his primary vulnerability.
- His relationship with Elizabeth is strained because of the affair; Elizabeth's cold, watchful manner toward him reflects her difficulty in forgiving him, contributing to the domestic tension that Abigail exploits.
- Proctor's initial response to the witch trials is one of cynical detachment — he is reluctant to become involved, partly because he fears exposing his own sin if he confronts Abigail directly.
- His decision to confront the court and expose Abigail represents the beginning of his heroic journey. He sacrifices his reputation and personal safety in the service of justice.
- His confession of adultery in court is an act of profound courage: he publicly destroys the reputation he has tried to protect throughout the play in order to expose Abigail's fraud.
- The reversal of this sacrifice — the court's refusal to believe him — intensifies his tragic situation: his honesty is not rewarded.
- His refusal to sign a false confession is the defining moment of his heroic transformation. He chooses death over a lie, asserting the integrity of his name and conscience.
- 'Because it is my name!' encapsulates the tragedy: Proctor's identity, integrity and moral worth are more valuable to him than survival.
- His final act is simultaneously a moral victory and a tragic defeat — he dies, but he dies as himself, with his goodness reclaimed.
- Candidates might argue that the play is equally concerned with the social and political critique of McCarthyism and mass hysteria, and that Proctor's personal journey is inseparable from these larger themes.

Credit valid alternative/mixed responses.
Refer to Sections B and C rubric (25 marks: Content 15 marks, Structure and Language 10 marks).

subQuestions.questionText: Place Extract I in context.
subQuestions.memoText:
The witch trials are in full progress. Abigail and the other girls have been accusing members of the Salem community of witchcraft. The court, presided over by Deputy Governor Danforth, has been accepting the girls' testimony as proof of witchcraft. John Proctor has come to court to challenge the proceedings and expose Abigail's fraud, bringing a deposition signed by ninety-one community members attesting to the good character of the accused.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss what Danforth's conduct in Extract I reveals about the abuse of authority.
subQuestions.memoText:
Danforth represents the abuse of authority in its most institutionalised form. Rather than pursuing truth and justice, he prioritises the court's reputation and the preservation of its authority. He treats dissent as a threat and uses his position to intimidate witnesses and suppress contradictory evidence. His logic — that anyone who questions the court is effectively 'against' it — exemplifies how authoritarian institutions close themselves to scrutiny. He is not motivated by malice alone but by a conviction that the court's legitimacy must be protected at all costs, which is itself a form of moral corruption.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.
subQuestions.topic: Drama – Authority and Abuse of Power

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how Miller uses the courtroom setting in Extract I to explore the theme of mass hysteria.
subQuestions.memoText:
The courtroom is the institutional home of mass hysteria in the play. Miller shows how hysteria is legitimised and amplified when it is endorsed by authority — the court gives the girls' accusations legal weight and social credibility. The setting creates a dynamic in which the accused are presumed guilty and the burden of proof falls on those who resist. The public nature of the court means that denials of witchcraft can be reinterpreted as signs of guilt. Miller uses the courtroom to show that mass hysteria does not remain a private phenomenon — it becomes dangerous when embedded in official institutions.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Critically discuss the dramatic irony present in Extract I.
subQuestions.memoText:
The central dramatic irony of Extract I — and the play — is that the audience knows Abigail is lying while the court, which is meant to determine truth, cannot or will not see it. This irony intensifies the tragedy: justice is not merely failing but is actively being used as an instrument of injustice. There is further irony in Proctor's situation: his attempt to tell the truth makes him appear more suspicious, while Abigail's lies appear credible. The courtroom — a space designed to reveal truth — becomes a space where truth is systematically suppressed.

Award 3 marks for a critical discussion.

subQuestions.questionText: Place Extract J in context.
subQuestions.memoText:
John Proctor has been arrested and condemned to hang for witchcraft. He has initially agreed to sign a false confession to save his life. However, when asked to name other witches and when confronted with the reality of his signed confession being posted publicly on the church door, he tears it up. He will be hanged at dawn. Elizabeth, brought to persuade him to confess, refuses to manipulate him. Hale pleads with Elizabeth to intervene.

Award 3 marks for three distinct points.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss what John Proctor's refusal to sign the confession reveals about his character in Extract J.
subQuestions.memoText:
Proctor's refusal reveals a character who has undergone a profound moral transformation. Earlier in the play, he is compromised by his adultery and reluctant to enter the public arena. Now, he chooses integrity over survival. His refusal is not reckless — he genuinely weighs the choice — but his conclusion is that a life purchased by a lie is not worth living. His insistence that his name not be defiled ('Because it is my name!') reveals that identity and moral consistency are, for him, more valuable than physical survival.

Award 3 marks for two ideas well discussed.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the significance of Elizabeth's response to Proctor in Extract J.
subQuestions.memoText:
Elizabeth's response is one of the most emotionally significant moments in the play. Rather than begging Proctor to live by signing the false confession, she accepts his decision and refuses to coerce him. Her words — 'He have his goodness now. God forbid I take it from him' — reveal her recognition that Proctor's integrity is more important than his survival. This response also marks her own moral development: she acknowledges that her coldness after the affair may have contributed to his initial weakness. Her acceptance transforms his death from mere execution into a redemptive act.

Award 3 marks for a well-developed discussion.

subQuestions.questionText: Using Extract J as a starting point, and drawing on your knowledge of the play as a whole, critically discuss whether The Crucible is ultimately a play about personal integrity or about social and political forces.
subQuestions.memoText:
PERSONAL INTEGRITY:
- The play's emotional and dramatic core is Proctor's personal journey toward self-reclamation. His choice to die rather than lie suggests that the play ultimately privileges individual conscience over collective pressure.
- Elizabeth, Giles Corey and Rebecca Nurse all represent characters whose integrity refuses to be compromised by social or political coercion.
- Miller presents individuals — not systems — as the ultimate moral agents: the play asks what a person is willing to die for.

SOCIAL AND POLITICAL FORCES:
- The play was written as an allegory for McCarthyism, making its political and social critique central to its meaning. Miller's primary target was the machinery of institutional persecution, not individual moral failure.
- The trials show how social forces — fear, reputation, religious authority — create conditions in which good people are destroyed regardless of their personal integrity.
- Even Proctor's heroic death does not stop the trials or save the innocent. Social forces outlast individual acts of integrity.
- The play can be read as a warning about what happens when social institutions abandon their commitment to truth and fairness.

Credit valid mixed responses.
Award 4 marks for a well-developed critical discussion that engages with the play as a whole.
